turns.prompt_text: I have many different kinds of batteries. Lithium, all sorts of different kinds. Some of them are the cylindrical shapes. They're around 1500-2000 milliamp hours. They're the kind that would go into, say, a Milwaukee battery pack. I would like to put them to use, but I'm unsure of how to go about that.
turns.response_html:
Based on your description—cylindrical, 1500–2000 mAh capacity, and commonly found in power tool packs like Milwaukee—you almost certainly have 18650 Lithium-Ion cells (18mm diameter, 65mm length). These are the "workhorses" of the DIY battery world.

Because these are likely salvaged or "high-discharge" cells (common in power tools), they are powerful but require strict safety protocols. Here is a guide on how to safely assess and repurpose them.

1. Safety & Identification

Before building anything, you must treat these cells with caution. Unlike standard AA batteries, lithium cells can vent flame or explode if shorted or mistreated.

  • Visual Inspection: Discard any cell with rust, dents, torn wrappers (the colored plastic coating), or signs of leakage.
  • The Wrapper: The entire metal body of the cylinder is the negative terminal, except for the very top button (positive). If the plastic wrapper is torn, the cell can short out easily. You can buy "18650 heat shrink" to re-wrap them.
  • Voltage Check: Use a multimeter.
    • > 3.0V: Good candidate.
    • 2.0V – 3.0V: Usable, but needs careful "recovery" charging.
    • < 2.0V: Hazardous. The internal chemistry may have degraded. Recycle these; do not attempt to charge.

2. Testing & Grading

You cannot mix "healthy" and "weak" batteries in a pack; the weak ones will fail and become a fire hazard. You need to categorize them.

  • Capacity Testing: You will need a specialized charger (like an Opus BT-C3100 or LiitoKala Lii-500). These chargers cycle the battery (charge-discharge-charge) to measure the actual remaining capacity in milliamp-hours (mAh).
  • Binning: Group batteries by similar capacity (e.g., a "1500-1600 mAh" bin and a "1900-2000 mAh" bin). Only build packs using cells from the same bin.

3. Connection Methods

How you connect them depends on your tools.

  • Battery Holders (Recommended for Beginners): These look like standard AA holders but are sized for 18650s. They use springs to hold the battery.
    • Pros: No welding required; easy to replace bad cells.
    • Cons: High resistance (not good for high-power applications like e-bikes).
  • Spot Welding: This uses a machine to weld nickel strips across the battery terminals.
    • Pros: Professional, low resistance, compact.
    • Cons: Requires buying a spot welder (~$50–$150).
  • Soldering (Warning): Do not solder directly to the battery terminals. The heat will damage the internal seals and chemistry before the solder melts properly. If you must solder, solder to the nickel strips after they are spot-welded, or use batteries that come with pre-tabbed solder tags.

4. The Brain: The BMS

You generally cannot use raw lithium batteries directly. You need a BMS (Battery Management System) board.

  • Function: It monitors the voltage of each cell group. It cuts power if a cell gets too low (preventing death) or too high (preventing fire).
  • Selection: If you put 3 batteries in a series to make 12V, you need a "3S BMS".

5. Project Ideas

Given that power tool batteries (like Milwaukee) are designed for high current (High Drain), they are excellent for:

  • USB Power Bank:
    • Build: Use 1 to 4 cells in parallel + a cheap "Power Bank Module" (PCB) from eBay/Amazon.
    • Result: A very high-capacity charger for your phone.
  • High-Powered LED Flashlight:
    • Many "tactical" flashlights (like the Convoy S2+) are designed specifically for a single 18650 cell.
  • Portable 12V Power Source:
    • Build: Connect 3 cells in series (3S) with a BMS.
    • Result: A lightweight battery pack that can power 12V LED strips, portable fans, or ham radios.
  • Power Wall (Advanced):
    • Some hobbyists collect hundreds of these to build massive energy storage for solar panels. This requires advanced knowledge of busbars and fusing.

Recommended First Step

If you want to start safely and cheaply, I recommend building a simple USB Power Bank.

  1. Buy a "DIY 18650 Power Bank Case" (usually $5–$10). These are empty plastic shells with the electronics already installed.
  2. Insert your tested 18650 cells (observing polarity!).
  3. Snap it shut.

This requires no soldering and puts your batteries to immediate use.

turns.prompt_text: I now have a 3D printer, as well as many multimeters. A 61-337 digital multimeter ideal. A soldering iron. And some resistors and capacitors. And plenty of copper wire. How could I create a battery pack for my Milwaukee tool?
turns.response_html:
You have the raw materials for a serious project, but there is one "hard truth" you need to know before you start: You cannot replicate the safety electronics (BMS) with just resistors and capacitors.

Milwaukee batteries contain a specialized circuit board that talks to the tool and the charger. Without it, the charger will refuse to charge your pack, and the tool may over-discharge the batteries, leading to fire risk.

However, you can build the physical battery pack using your 3D printer and tools, provided you buy or salvage one specific component: a replacement Milwaukee BMS/Case shell (approx. $15 online).

Here is how to execute this build using your specific gear.

Phase 1: The "Copper Wire" & 3D Printer Method

Since you don't have a spot welder (which uses nickel strips), you have to solder. Soldering directly to batteries is dangerous because heat damages the internal seals. Your Solution: Use your 3D printer to create a "soldering jig" and use the "Tesla-style" fuse wire method.

1. Print a Cell Holder (The Jig) Instead of gluing batteries together, print a custom 18650 spacer/holder.

  • Search for: "18650 cell holder offset" or "honeycomb 18650 spacer".
  • Why: This keeps the cells perfectly spaced and provides a structure to mount your copper wire busbars away from the battery terminals, reducing heat transfer.

2. Create Copper "Busbars" You have plenty of copper wire.

  • Strip the insulation off your thickest copper wire (12 or 14 gauge is best).
  • Straighten it and lay it across the top of your 3D-printed holder, aligned with the battery rows (but not touching the terminals yet).
  • The Trick: Do not solder this thick wire directly to the battery. It requires too much heat.

3. The "Fuse Wire" Connection

  • Take a single thin strand of copper wire (or a resistor leg).
  • Solder one end to the Battery Terminal (Quickly! < 2 seconds).
  • Solder the other end to your thick Copper Busbar.
  • Benefit: If a battery shorts out, this thin wire acts as a fuse and melts, disconnecting the bad cell and preventing an explosion. This is how Tesla builds their battery packs.

Phase 2: The Electronics (The "Brain")

You mentioned resistors and capacitors. While you can't build the main BMS with these, you can use your Ideal 61-337 multimeter to ensure the pack works safely.

1. Voltage Matching (Crucial Step) Before connecting any batteries together, they must be at the exact same voltage.

  • Set your Ideal 61-337 to DC Volts.
  • Measure every single 18650 cell.
  • Rule: All cells in a parallel group must be within 0.05V of each other (e.g., 3.60V and 3.65V is okay; 3.60V and 4.00V is dangerous).
  • If they don't match: Charge the lower ones individually until they match.

2. Wiring the BMS You will need to buy a "Milwaukee M18 PCB Case Kit" (widely available on eBay/Amazon). It comes with the plastic shell and the circuit board.

  • M18 Configuration: 5 Series (5S). You will need 5 groups of batteries connected in a chain.
  • Wiring: Connect your copper busbars to the B-, B1, B2, B3, B4, and B+ solder points on the BMS board.

Phase 3: Assembly & The "Smoke Test"

  1. Print the Case: If you didn't buy a kit, you can 3D print the entire battery housing.
    • Note: Printing the latch mechanism is tricky. It's often better to print an "Adapter" (e.g., a belt clip that holds your big battery pack) and run a cable to an old "dead" Milwaukee battery shell plugged into the tool.
  2. Check Resistance: Use your multimeter to check for shorts between your positive and negative busbars before you attach the BMS.
  3. Final Voltage Check: Measure the total voltage at the main terminals.
    • For M18: Should be between 18V and 21V.
    • For M12: Should be between 10.8V and 12.6V.

Summary Checklist

  • Do Not: Try to build the protection circuit with capacitors/resistors.
  • Do: Buy a cheap "M18 BMS PCB replacement".
  • Do: Use your 3D printer to make spacers/holders.
  • Do: Use your copper wire as main "Busbars" but connect them to the cells with thin "fuse wire" to minimize heat.

Your inventory—specifically the Bambu Lab A1, Ideal 61-337, and copper wire—changes the strategy. You have the tools to build a professional-grade external battery system or a careful internal rebuild.

Here is the specific plan to build a Milwaukee-compatible pack using your current materials.

The "Space Constraint" Problem

Standard Milwaukee cases are injection-molded to fit cells exactly. There is almost zero room for thick copper wire or "Tesla-style" fuse wires inside a standard shell. If you try to stuff a copper-wire build into a standard case, it won't close.

The Solution: Use your 3D printer to build an External "Backpack" Battery. Instead of trying to cram cells into a tiny tool casing, you will:

  1. Print an "M18 Adapter" that clicks into your tool.
  2. Build a larger, custom battery box (wearable or desktop) using your copper wire method.
  3. Connect them via a heavy-gauge cable. This allows you to use many more cells (e.g., 10 or 20 for huge runtime) and safely use your copper wire/fuse construction.

Step 1: The 3D Prints (Search Terms)

Since I cannot send files directly, search for these exact terms on Printables or Thingiverse. Your Bambu A1 will handle these easily (use PETG if possible, as PLA might melt in a hot car).

  • For the Tool Connection: Search "Milwaukee M18 Battery Adapter".
    • Look for: A design that uses "spade connectors" or "crimp terminals."
    • Goal: This part clicks into your drill and gives you two wires (Positive/Negative) coming out.
  • For the Battery Assembly: Search "18650 Solder Jig".
    • Recommended Model: Look for "18650 SOLDER JIG by Emmy Bear 3D" or similar.
    • Why: This holds the cells tight so you can solder without them rolling around.
  • For the External Case: Search "Rugged Battery Box".
    • Goal: A box to hold your finished pack.

Step 2: The "Copper & Fuse" Build (Tesla Style)

This is the safest way to build a pack without a spot welder.

  1. Print the Jig: Print a 5x2 (or larger) cell holder.
  2. Busbar Prep:
    • Strip your thick copper wire (12 or 14 AWG).
    • Lay two straight strands along the length of the holder (one for Positive row, one for Negative).
    • CRITICAL: Do not let the thick wire touch the battery terminals directly. It should hover slightly above or to the side.
  3. The Fuse Wire:
    • Take a single thin strand of copper wire (unwind a standard stranded wire to get one hair-thin strand).
    • Solder one end to the battery terminal (Quickly! < 2 seconds).
    • Solder the other end to the thick copper busbar.
    • Why: If a battery fails/shorts, this thin hair will melt instantly, disconnecting the bad cell and preventing a fire.

Step 3: Wiring for 18V (5S Configuration)

To make it run a Milwaukee tool, you need 18 Volts.

  • You need 5 groups of batteries in series.
  • Group 1: Connect Neg(-) of Group 1 to Pos(+) of Group 2.
  • Group 2: Connect Neg(-) of Group 2 to Pos(+) of Group 3... and so on up to Group 5.
  • Your main Positive comes from Group 1, and Main Negative from Group 5.

Step 4: The BMS (The One Part You Must Buy)

You still need a 5S BMS Board (about $10 on Amazon/eBay).

  • Wiring: Solder the "Sense Wires" from the BMS to each of the 5 connections between your battery groups.
  • Safety: This board will prevent you from over-draining the pack and destroying your recycled cells.

Step 5: Final Assembly

  1. Put your "Copper Wire Pack" into your 3D printed external box.
  2. Run a thick 12-gauge cable from the BMS output to the 3D Printed M18 Adapter.
  3. Click the adapter into your drill.
  4. Clip the battery box to your belt or set it on the bench.

Result: A tool that weighs 2 lbs less (because the battery is on your belt) and runs for 3x longer than a standard pack.
